## Create your first map

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(bloomr)
bloom_map()
```

1. Select **Bloom counties** to spread the counties apart.
2. Select a county and choose **Bloom municipalities** to see its smaller areas.
3. Drag a shape to move it. The dot and dotted line show where it came from.
4. Choose **Back** to return one level.

Hover over an area to see its name. By default, labels stay hidden so the map remains clear. Original county and local-area lines remain visible.

You can also use the included Texas map:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
bloom_map("tx")
```

## Choose the levels to explore

For a state-to-county map that stops at counties, set `view = "state_county"`:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
bloom_map("nj", view = "state_county")
```

To start at a county and bloom its municipalities directly, name that county:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
bloom_map("nj", view = "county_local", county = "bergen")
```

You can also use the county GEOID (`"34003"`). For Texas, the second view
blooms county subdivisions, for example
`bloom_map("tx", view = "county_local", county = "harris")`.
Both views accept numeric data using the IDs at the level being displayed.

## Add numeric values

Use a data frame with unique geographic IDs and one numeric measure:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
rates <- data.frame(
  geoid = c("34003", "34013", "34021"),
  rate = c(12.5, 18.2, 9.3)
)

bloom_check_data(rates, value = "rate", geography = "nj")
bloom_map("nj", data = rates, key = "geoid", value = "rate")
```

Keep IDs such as GEOIDs as character strings to preserve leading zeros. Areas with no matched value remain distinct from areas with numeric values.

## Choose the appearance

```{r, eval=FALSE}
bloom_map("nj", labels = "selected")
bloom_map("nj", theme = "dark")
bloom_map("nj", local_boundaries = FALSE)
```

Light mode, dots, dotted connectors, and both types of original boundary lines are on by default. Use **Display** on the map to change lines or labels interactively.

## Where to use it

`bloom_map()` works in the RStudio Viewer and HTML reports. In Shiny, use `bloomOutput()` with `renderBloom()`. See [Use Bloom in Shiny](using-in-shiny.html) for a complete example.

## Supported maps and data

The package includes New Jersey and Texas geography and accepts your own numeric indicator data for these maps. You can also bring your own polygon boundaries using an `sf` object or GeoJSON file. See [Using your own data](using-your-own-data.html). For an HTML report that opens independently, use `bloom_map(portable = TRUE)` before saving the widget.
